rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1, 2.3, 3 - own airborne hyperspectral/thermal campaigns on three dates in 2012 over 192 olive plots, field albedometer measurements, and METRIC model runs at pixel sizes from 5 m to 1 km (Tables 1-4).
rows.notes: The study only estimates ETc/water requirements with METRIC from airborne imagery and evaluates how the energy balance components change with pixel size (Rn and G near insensitive; H up to 17% and LE/ETc up to 23% divergence at resolutions coarser than 30 m). It does not test any irrigation management strategy, nor measure water productivity or water savings; the passage's effect (irrigation strategies increasing water productivity) is only implied in the Discussion as a use of the estimates. Moreover, the ETc output is never compared with field ET measurements (only albedo was validated against albedometers), so even the ET estimate itself is not checked against the real system. Study supports only the precondition (estimating water requirements).

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1, 2.3, 3 - own airborne hyperspectral/thermal campaigns on three dates in 2012 over 192 olive plots, field albedometer measurements, and METRIC model runs at pixel sizes from 5 m to 1 km (Tables 1-4).
rows.notes: No yield or fruit/oil quality data are reported anywhere in the study; it quantifies only energy balance components, ETc and Kco from METRIC at different spatial resolutions. The study provides the precondition (remote-sensing estimates of orchard water requirements) but no result on irrigation strategies optimising olive yield or quality. ETc estimates were also not validated against field ET measurements.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). The study is a methodological sensitivity analysis of METRIC to pixel size over olive orchards in southern Spain; its only field validation concerns surface albedo (Landsat vs albedometers, Fig. 3), not ET, water productivity or yield.
